A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is a trade-off between defence against grazing (i.e. being eaten less) and competitive ability (i.e. growing faster in nutrient–limited conditions) in the alga C. vulgaris.
the evolution of defence against predation in unicellular organisms can be rapid and complex, with the potential to alter the ecological dynamics of the predator–prey interaction.
the trade–off between grazing resistance and competitive ability can be a major factor in determining the evolutionary trajectories of populations of C. vulgaris.
The main takeaway from our work is that

even in the simple system we studied, the evolutionary dynamics of defence are not independent from other fitness components, and that trade–offs can play a key role in shaping the evolutionary trajectories of defence.
trade–offs between defence against herbivores and competitive ability may be a common feature of ecological communities.
trade–offs between defence against grazing, competitive ability, and other fitness components can be important even in simple unicellular organisms.
